line: Did you know, the statue of Alfred the Great in Southwark stands on Roman legs?
fact: The legs of Southwark's Alfred the Great are Roman, from about AD 100. The top half was added around 1800, which makes it probably London's oldest outdoor statue.
source: Wikipedia: Statue of Alfred the Great, Southwark

line: Did you know, the world's first cash machine was in Enfield?
fact: The world's first cash machine opened at Barclays in Enfield in June 1967. You used a paper voucher bought in advance, and could take out £10 at most.

line: Did you know, Barnet Gate was once named after the monster in Beowulf?
fact: To the Anglo-Saxons, Barnet Gate was Grendel's Gate, after the monster in the poem Beowulf. A charter from about 975 uses the name.

line: Did you know, Foyles protected its roof in the Blitz with copies of Mein Kampf?
fact: In the Blitz, Foyles bookshop covered its roof with copies of Hitler's Mein Kampf instead of sandbags. Newsreels showed a clerk stacking them up.

line: Did you know, the Strand's maypole ended up holding Isaac Newton's telescope?
fact: A famous maypole stood where St Mary le Strand is now. In 1717 Isaac Newton bought it to hold up a telescope, then the largest in the world.

line: Did you know, a one-legged man rode the Underground's first escalators to show they were safe?
fact: The Underground's first escalators opened at Earl's Court in 1911. A one-legged engineer, Bumper Harris, rode them on the first day to reassure passengers.

line: Did you know, Dick Whittington gave London a toilet with 128 seats?
fact: Dick Whittington paid for a public toilet by the Thames with 128 seats, 64 for men and 64 for women. The tide washed it out twice a day.

line: Did you know, the world's first coal-fired public power station was on Holborn Viaduct?
fact: The world's first coal-fired power station for public use was at 57 Holborn Viaduct, built by Thomas Edison's company. New York got its own afterwards.

line: Did you know, a telephone exchange off Whitehall hides a way into secret tunnels?
fact: The BT telephone exchange in Craig's Court, off Whitehall, holds one of the entrances to the secret government tunnels under central London.

line: Did you know, the first baby born on the Underground arrived at Elephant & Castle?
fact: In May 1924 a girl was born at Elephant & Castle, the first baby born on the Underground. The railway's chairman, Lord Ashfield, became her godfather, and she got his name as a middle name.

line: Did you know, until 1999 the Queen was the only woman allowed in the Lord's Pavilion during play?
fact: Until 1999, women weren't allowed in the Lord's Pavilion during play. The one exception was the Queen, the club's patron.

line: Did you know, the Bomber Command Memorial's roof is made from a crashed bomber?
fact: The roof of the Bomber Command Memorial in Green Park is made from a Halifax bomber that crashed in Belgium in 1944. It was pulled out of a swamp in 1997.

line: Did you know, wood from Ruislip helped build the Tower of London?
fact: Timber from Ruislip Woods went into the Tower of London in 1339, Windsor Castle in 1344 and the Palace of Westminster in 1346.

line: Did you know, Churchill hid in a closed tube station he called the Barn?
fact: Down Street station closed in 1932. In the war Churchill and his cabinet sheltered there until the Cabinet War Rooms were ready, and he called it the Barn.

line: Did you know, a fifth of all animal war heroes with the Dickin Medal are buried in Ilford?
fact: Thirteen animals awarded the Dickin Medal, the animals' medal for bravery, are buried at Ilford Animal Cemetery. That's a fifth of every animal ever given it.

line: Did you know, Britain's first moving pictures were shown on Regent Street?
fact: In February 1896, the Regent Street Cinema showed a short film by the Lumière brothers. It was the first motion picture ever shown in the UK.

line: Did you know, London's first house with a telephone was at Crooked Billet in Wimbledon?
fact: The first house in London to have a telephone was at Crooked Billet in Wimbledon.

line: Did you know, a First World War hospital on Endell Street was run entirely by women?
fact: In the First World War, a military hospital at 36 Endell Street was staffed entirely by women. Two suffragist doctors ran it, and it treated 24,000 patients.

line: Did you know, a bridge in Kingston was once a football goal?
fact: Every Shrove Tuesday, Kingston played a football match in the town centre. Clattern Bridge was one team's goal, and Kingston Bridge was the other's.

line: Did you know, Pall Mall is named after a game like croquet?
fact: Pall Mall is named after pall-mall, a game like croquet, played here on a long, narrow court in the 17th century. The street was built over the old court in 1661.

line: Did you know, the statue of James II outside the National Gallery once lay in the weeds?
fact: The statue of James II outside the National Gallery was taken down to make room for Edward VII's coronation stands. It lay on its back in the weeds until 1903.
source: Wikipedia: Statue of James II, Trafalgar Square

line: Did you know, the statue of George V by Parliament spent the war in a quarry?
fact: The statue of George V opposite the House of Lords was carved in a Portland quarry. It spent the Second World War hidden in one of the quarry's tunnels.
source: Wikipedia: Statue of George V, Westminster
